clue.text: Iron Man is a woman (6)

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron, from the Latin ferrum
a man is a male of the species

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M does all the misdirection: 'Iron Man' reads as the Marvel hero, and the two words have to be prised apart and taken one at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names any person of the sex that bears young, so it covers 'woman' exactly, with a reach that takes in other species too.

clue.text: Satisfactory punishment (4)

blocks.note: the everyday 'that's OK by me' sense: acceptable, good enough
the sum a court makes you pay for an offence

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses sit side by side with nothing between them, which is the whole trick of the type: the clue reads as one phrase about a sentence being reasonable.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the approving adjective, acceptable or good enough; the other is the money penalty a court imposes, which is a punishment.

clue.text: Ingredient of comfort food covering rear end of Shakespearean (7)

definitions.note: The adjective stands in for a proper noun: the setter means a figure out of the plays, and the answer is that figure's name rather than a description of anything.

indicators.note: In a down entry one piece covers another by lying on top of it, so the first chunk sits above the second.

blocks.note: mac is the macaroni of macaroni cheese, the comfort dish it is named for
duff is American slang for the backside — 'get off your duff'

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface warns you that a name is coming: 'Shakespearean' looks like an adjective describing the food, and two slang words underneath it hide a thane.
explanation.definitionFit: Macduff is the thane who kills Macbeth, so the adjective points at him as a figure out of the plays rather than describing anything.

clue.text: Celebrated rugby player offside (8)

indicators.note: The instruction is the front of the word: milk that has gone off has turned, and the four letters behind it turn out of the order given.

blocks.note: a Lion is a player picked for the British and Irish Lions, the touring team drawn from four countries
four letters resorted to close the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Offside' is one word in the clue and two separate jobs in the parse; the rugby surface is there precisely to stop you splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: To lionise someone is to make a celebrity of them, so the past participle matches 'celebrated' in both sense and tense.

clue.text: Criticise character from Athens, thus creating sort of poetry (3,5)

blocks.note: to rap someone is to criticise them sharply — a rap on the knuckles
mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
sic is Latin for 'thus', printed in brackets to say a quoted mistake really was there

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about an Athenian being insulted; the answer is a modern genre, and the hinge between them is the word editors print after somebody else's misspelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Rap is metrical verse, rhymed and stressed and delivered over a beat, so 'sort of poetry' names the category it belongs to.

clue.text: Amoebae and such travelled nautical miles, giving up sex in retrospect (11)

indicators.note: Anything that has travelled has left the position it started in, and so has every letter here.
To give something up is to surrender it, so whatever is named next is handed over before the shuffle.
To see something in retrospect is to look back at it, and the two letters are taken back to front.

blocks.note: thirteen letters to start from, two of which will not survive
'it' is the old euphemism for sex — 'they were at it' — and turned round it is the pair that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sea voyage and none of it is a measurement: the only instruction in the clue is that a small word leaves before the letters are shaken. 'It' for sex is worth filing away.
explanation.definitionFit: Animalcules is the old naturalists' word for microscopic creatures, amoebae among them, so the definition names them by an example plus 'and such'.

clue.text: Lower, but greater (6)

blocks.note: the comparative of 'mean' in its base sense: more ignoble, more shabby, further down
American colloquial 'mean' is praise — a mean fastball, a mean chilli — and its comparative points the opposite way

explanation.walkthrough: One word pulled in two directions, base and admirable, and 'but' is the setter promising you the contradiction is deliberate rather than a slip.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is 'more base or ignoble'; the other is the colloquial praise in 'plays a mean guitar', where the word means formidably good.

clue.text: Originally, source (excessively loud noise) was a sub (5,2)

indicators.note: The origin of a word is where it begins, so only the opening letter of the word after it is taken.

blocks.note: the first letter of 'source'
too much is excessively much
a din is a racket loud enough to drown out talk

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is the giveaway once you spot it: the aside is not describing the source, it is two more chunks of the build. And 'sub' here means substitute, not sandwich or submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand in for someone is to substitute for them, which is what a sub does; clue and answer are both in the past tense.

clue.text: Hustler’s damage includes train wreck (3,6)

indicators.note: What a thing includes is held inside it, so the letters named next go within the ones named first.
A wreck is what is left when something is smashed apart, and these letters arrive in pieces.

blocks.note: 'what's the damage?' asks what something cost
five letters smashed out of shape and dropped in after the first two

explanation.walkthrough: 'Train wreck' is one phrase in the surface and two separate jobs in the parse; hustler is wanted in its swindling sense, not the sense of somebody who works fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A con artist makes a living out of confidence tricks, which is what a hustler does — the swindler, not the energetic worker.

clue.text: Snack: portion of spinach ossobuco (6)

indicators.note: A portion is served up just as it came off the larger thing, so what is wanted is an unbroken run of the letters that follow rather than a word meaning them.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters run across the gap between the two dishes

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes those two words read as a dish on a menu, which is exactly why the join between them is easy to skate straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: Nachos are tortilla chips under melted cheese, eaten between meals, and a plateful of them counts as one snack.

clue.text: Photo, a character from long ago: outspoken rogue (8)

indicators.note: Spoken out is spoken aloud, so the piece in front of it is written the way it sounds rather than the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: pic is the everyday short form of picture
the clue's own article, taken at face value
a rune is a letter of the old Germanic alphabet — a character from long ago — and saying it aloud respells it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outspoken' looks like a description of the rogue and is really doing sound duty, which is why the old letter has to be said before it is written.
explanation.definitionFit: A picaroon is a rogue or brigand — the word comes from the Spanish pícaro, the trickster hero of picaresque novels.

clue.text: Engaged in drink, CIA annulled cryptic system of old Rome (6,8)

indicators.note: To be engaged in something is to be taken up inside it, which is where this batch of letters ends up.
A cryptic message has been put into code, and the plainest code of all just scrambles the order of the letters.

blocks.note: a jar is a pint of beer — 'fancy a jar?'
eleven letters, the agency's initials among them, all resorted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Annulled' wants to be an instruction to delete something; it is fodder. The drink is split into its first letter and its last two, and everything else goes in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The Julian calendar is the year-length reform Julius Caesar imposed in 46 BC, so the phrase names Rome's own way of reckoning dates.

clue.text: Singer wanting cabbage to whip up piece in advance (3,4,4)

indicators.note: In a down entry, up sends the letters back the way they came, from the foot of the answer towards its head.
To be in advance of something is to be ahead of it, so these two chunks are placed before the cabbage rather than after it.

blocks.note: to tan a hide is to whip it, and those three letters then climb
the piece a whole game of chess is played to protect
cole is the cabbage family — the cole of coleslaw

explanation.walkthrough: Cabbage, whipping and a piece all sound like one kitchen scene; only the singer at the front tells you they are three separate chunks of somebody's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Nat King Cole was the velvet-voiced American who recorded 'Unforgettable', so the definition names him by his profession.

clue.text: Plunderers’ music fest in part of Winchester? (5,5)

blocks.note: to rifle a drawer is to go through it and take what you want, which is what a plunderer does
Woodstock gave festivals their ending, and -stock has been stuck on the back of them ever since

explanation.walkthrough: Winchester wants to be the cathedral city and is the American gun, and a plunderers' festival is a joke name built on the back of Woodstock.
explanation.definitionFit: A Winchester is the lever-action rifle of the American West, and the stock is the wooden shoulder-piece at its back — one named part of the gun.

clue.text: Don’t play at stalls where Yanks relieve themselves? (4,5)

blocks.note: a rest is the mark in a score telling the player to stay silent for a beat
an engine that stalls comes to a halt

explanation.walkthrough: The stalls are a theatre's seats in the surface and an engine's dying in the parse, and the question mark is there because the definition is a joke about American highway signs.
explanation.definitionFit: A rest stop is the American roadside pull-in with lavatories, so the definition names them by the thing travellers actually stop for.

clue.text: Prey for an aardvark: one Contra (4)

blocks.note: the aardvark's whole diet, and the crossword's standard worker
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: The capital C is surface only — it points at the Nicaraguan Contras of the 1980s — and the word underneath it is just the Latin for 'against'.
explanation.definitionFit: Contra and anti are the Latin and Greek prefixes of opposition, so the two are straight synonyms: both mean 'against'.

clue.text: Drunken peer falls into brewski-chugging contraption in drinkers’ diversion (4,4)

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and these four letters cannot hold their line either.
Whatever falls into something ends up inside it, so the shuffled letters land within the other word.

blocks.note: a bong is the tube-and-funnel gadget a drink is poured down in one go, and brewski is US slang for a beer
the lord's four letters, tipped over and dropped in after the first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunken peer' reads as one phrase and is really an instruction plus the material it works on, and the contraption is split open to take the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer pong is the party game of throwing a ping-pong ball into cups of beer, which makes it exactly a diversion for drinkers.

clue.text: God backflips into canal (4)

indicators.note: A backflip takes you head over heels, and an across entry that flips like that is read from its right-hand end.

blocks.note: the chief god of the Greeks, the thrower of thunderbolts

explanation.walkthrough: 'God' opening the clue reads as the Christian one, which is exactly why the Olympian who fits — turned end for end — takes a moment to find.
explanation.definitionFit: The Suez Canal is the ship channel cut through Egypt between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, so 'canal' names it by example.

clue.text: E, for Einstein? (7)

blocks.note: one letter, and the one his surname begins with: in crossword terms, the head of Einstein
the question mark asks you to take him as an example, and what the world takes him as an example of is brains

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are hiding in plain sight: E is Einstein's head, and the sort of head Einstein is famous for having is an egg one — EGGHEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: the man is the byword for an intellectual, and 'head' is the half of the word that single letter supplies.

clue.text: Lifted off around two, say: it may require a shot (5,5)

indicators.note: Something off is not as it should be, and these six letters are not in the order they should be.
What goes around something stands on both sides of it, so the shuffled letters open and close the answer.
'Say' means 'for example', flagging that the number given is only one instance of the word wanted.

blocks.note: six letters rearranged, and they end up split in two
two is an even number, one instance among many

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted off' reads as a take-off and is really fodder plus its shuffle; the shot is the athlete's iron ball, not a drink, an injection or anything on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A field event is the throwing and jumping half of an athletics meeting, and the shot put is one of them — hence the ball it may require.

clue.text: € is based on this Greek character harboured by lone lunatic (7)

indicators.note: To harbour someone is to shelter them inside your own house, so the piece before it goes within the piece after.
A lunatic is out of his right mind, and the letters he governs come out in the wrong order.

blocks.note: four letters resorted, ending up on either side of the middle
psi is the Greek letter shaped like a trident, and it goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' wants to be the definition and is the wordplay — the letter it names is a different one, tucked inside. The euro sign really was drawn from a Greek letter with two bars added.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro symbol was designed as this Greek letter with two parallel strokes through it, so 'based on this' points straight at it.

clue.text: 75% of plátanos turned into something romantic (6)

indicators.note: Three quarters of an eight-letter word is six letters, and it is the opening pair that gets dropped here.
Turned means those letters are read the other way round, from the last of them back to the first.

blocks.note: the Spanish for bananas, minus its opening pair

explanation.walkthrough: The italics tell you the word is foreign and the arithmetic tells you how much of it to keep; 'into' is only a link, not an instruction to insert anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is an instrumental piece, and the Romantic composers wrote them by the hundred, so the definition points at it by example.

clue.text: Get ogress irritated and annoyed with symbol (2,7,5)

indicators.note: Somebody irritated is worked up and will not sit still, and nor will these nine letters.

blocks.note: nine letters shaken up, and they come out as a saint's name with a possessive on the end
cross is the everyday British word for annoyed

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has one angry monster and one angry person; the answer is a flag. 'Annoyed' is the word that has to be read as a noun rather than an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The St George's Cross — a red cross on a white ground — is the national flag and emblem of England, so 'symbol' names it as one.

clue.text: Killer imprisoned in Windsor Castle (4)

indicators.note: A prisoner is shut inside walls, and these letters are shut inside the two words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters straddle the space between the royal house and its home

explanation.walkthrough: Windsor Castle is one place-name in the surface and two words to be read across in the parse; the killer is the whale, not a murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: An orca is the killer whale, and 'killer' on its own is the standard short name for the species rather than for a person who kills.

clue.text: Smooth talker on X, say (8)

blocks.note: the stock phrase pairs 'smooth' with this word for a slick, plausible mover who plays people rather than machines
the multiplication sign is one example of the symbols that act on the numbers in an equation

explanation.walkthrough: The same noun twice over: the person who works an angle, and the sign that works on numbers. 'On X' looks like the social network and is only holding the sentence together.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the slick manipulator of the stock phrase; the other is the mathematical sign, the × that acts on the numbers around it.

clue.text: Arrest in general location reversed (6)

indicators.note: This little word is doing the hiding: what is wanted sits inside the phrase that follows, not beside it.
Reversed means the run of letters is read the other way, from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters cross the gap between the two words, though not in the direction you are reading

explanation.walkthrough: 'General' and 'location' both offer themselves as definitions of a place, and neither is one: the two words are there to be read through, backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To collar someone is to seize them by the neck and hold them, which is police slang for making an arrest.

clue.text: Sob stories in Slate? (3,5)

indicators.note: The second word is to be found inside the magazine's own five letters, resorted — a loose signal that the question mark owns up to.

blocks.note: a sob story is a sad one, so this word does double duty — definition and wordplay at once
the American magazine's five letters, resorted

explanation.walkthrough: The clue defines itself twice: the whole phrase means the answer, and its first word is also a chunk of the build. The italics mark Slate as a title, not a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A sob story is exactly a sad tale — the hard-luck account told to win sympathy — so the two plural phrases are straight synonyms.

clue.text: Turkish bigwig covers arse, it may be hidden (6)

indicators.note: One thing covers another by lying over it on both sides, so the word before wraps round the word after.

blocks.note: an aga was a commander or grandee of the Ottoman empire
your end is your rear, the part you sit on

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase rather than a word: what may be hidden is a plan, and the adjective that always goes in front of it is the whole point of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden agenda is the stock phrase for an ulterior motive, so the definition identifies the word by the company it keeps.
